payload.body: Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

In any given language, the syntactic rule subsystem is a component part inside the whole grammar rule system, alongside the phonological, morphological, and semantic portions — exactly Law 10 part-of, with the note pinning both endpoint senses correctly against the accepted carves. This is also the correct type for the relation the twin edge misclassifies as INSTANCE_OF: a component part is not an instance of the whole.

A parameter value is not a substrate. The accepted PLV carve lists 'analysis/synthesis window length and hop size' among its parameters — length and hop, not shape. Window shape is a design choice among tapers (Hann, Hamming, Blackman, rectangular, other COLA windows). Removal test against the target actually filed: remove the Hann function and the vocoder still operates with any other taper; what changes is the spectral-leakage/overlap-add trade-off — a design-level change, not an operational stop (partial loss is not DEPENDS_ON). The note's argument is circular: it asserts the frames 'lose their defined spectral leakage properties and overlap-add consistency', but frames defined with a substitute taper have their own defined properties and their own COLA consistency — no frame-level failure that a substitute could not repair is identified. 'The specific window shape used' is a standard implementation choice, not a constitutive requirement of the construct.

INSTANCE_OF runs specific to its nearest accepted kind (Law 9), and the nearest kind of a syntactic rule system is not grammar. Per the accepted carves, grammar is the WHOLE — the complete rule system of a language, explicitly including the syntactic, morphological, phonological, and semantic portions — and syntax is a component part of that whole. A component is not an instance of its whole: the note itself calls syntax 'a specific component', which is the part-of relation, and that relation is filed separately (grammar CONTAINS syntax). Instances of grammar are specific languages' complete rule systems; instances of syntax are specific syntactic systems or patterns (a particular language's word-order system; hypotaxis, parataxis). Whole is not an instance of its own component; the pinned narrowing does not hold.

Changed from STRIKE to ADVANCE on the confirmed record. I had treated 'language is a system of symbolic signs' as a disqualifying identity appeal; the board's own accepted record says otherwise. writing DEPENDS_ON symbol stands ACCEPTED, and writing is by definition a system of graphic symbols — the identical shape: a made system whose elements are instances of the symbol kind, operating by sign-manipulation. The symbol kind is independent and broader than language (traffic signs, mathematical and musical notation stand without language; symbol carries its own accepted dependency, symbol DEPENDS_ON semiosis), so this is the meter-to-beat component shape — a system structured over an independent unit kind — not a tautology: remove the kind of representation-that-stands-for-something-beyond-itself and the encode/transmit/decode operation the accepted definition carves is impossible, while the kind itself survives without language. My identity-appeal objection proved too much: it would strike the accepted writing-to-symbol edge as well. The note's pinned sense (symbol as the abstract sign-representation relation, constitutive of language as a symbolic system) is a sense the target's accepted definition supports.

Changed from ADVANCE to STRIKE on the better argument. The syntax entry's accepted definition is the BROAD formal kind: well-formedness rules for elements (words, symbols, notes, tokens) 'within a formal domain' — language, code, music, and other formal sign systems. Part-of at the entry level must hold of the KIND, and it does not: the kind's non-linguistic members (musical syntax, code syntax) are not parts of any grammar, so the syntax kind overlaps the grammar kind across the language domain rather than sitting inside it. The note's pin — 'syntax as its sentence-structure subcomponent' — names the language-domain instance of the kind, an instance-level fact (a given language's syntactic subsystem is a part of that language's grammar), not a sense the target's accepted definition supports; an instance-level part does not license the entry-level claim (Law 11d). The accepted sibling ladder confirms the board's grain: linguistics CONTAINS syntax and syntax INSTANCE_OF linguistics both stand ACCEPTED — syntax sits under linguistics, not under grammar. The honest structure requires an intermediate node: an entry for the linguistic-sense syntax kind, to which grammar CONTAINS would correctly attach, with that node INSTANCE_OF the broad syntax kind. STRIKE.

Changed from STRIKE to ADVANCE on the better argument. I had read the target as a map over natural territory and treated the note's removal as applied to the territory; that was the wrong grain. The accepted definition carves the CATEGORY: 'the human-constructed category for the set of mental processes — perception, memory, reasoning, problem-solving, and attention.' The note's pinned sense — the cognitive mechanisms of language use (perception, production, acquisition, representation) — is exactly the category's members in the language domain; perception and representation appear in the definition's own member list, so the pinned sense is one the target's accepted definition supports. Strip the category and the discipline loses its object: its questions ('how does the mind process sentences?'), its experimental interpretations, and its identity all stand or fall with the category; what remains is the genus (general/behavioral linguistics), not the discipline. That is an operational stop, not a partial loss — my earlier 'the territory remains' point proves too little, because the natural processes that remain are not the discipline's objects; the objects are the categorized processes. The board's accepted pattern confirms the shape: psycholinguistics's first leg, DEPENDS_ON language (its domain), stands ACCEPTED, and this edge is the second, distinguishing leg to the 'psycho-' half of the discipline — subfield DEPENDS_ON its distinctive subject is the accepted shape here, not the forbidden 'as a concept it needs cognition' appeal.

The removal test is misapplied. Removing cognition does not stop psycholinguistics from operating as a discipline; it only removes its subject matter. Law 8b distinguishes operational collapse from mere loss of sayability. Psycholinguistics as a made construct continues to exist as a research program, methods, publications even if cognition were absent. The claim confuses subject matter with operational dependency, and Law 2b bars meta-level dependencies on cognition for every map. The edge is meta-level, not object-level.
